processing: Small-leaf black tea made in imitation of Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong outside the Tongmu area; usually with pine smoke, as with other souchong in that style.
harvest_season: Not specifically recorded; follows the local black tea season, with spring typically the main picking.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted strips, typical of smoked souchong-style tea.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber, clear when well made.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaves of medium size.
taste_profile: Usually a plainer version of the Tongmu style: pine smoke, where used, over a malty sweet body, with less depth than good Zheng Shan tea.

brewing.notes: General advice for souchong-style black tea. It takes hot water and a Western pot well; go shorter if the smoke turns harsh.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under this name, since few shops advertise a tea as an imitation; it more often appears as generic souchong or Lapsang. As is usual for this kind of black tea, buy a recent harvest; smoke fades slowly but the tea has no special reason to be aged.
description:
Waishan Xiaozhong, 'outer-mountain souchong', is a label of contrast. Real Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong comes from around Tongmu in the Wuyi Mountains; anything made in its image elsewhere falls under this name, also called Rengong Xiaozhong.

The places named are Zhenghe, Tanyang, Beiling, Pingnan, Gutian and Sha county in Fujian, along with Yanshan in Jiangxi. The imitation aims at Tongmu's style, and traditional accounts rate its quality lower.

Expect a simpler cup than the Tongmu original, with more of the plain malt and sweetness of a local black tea and, where used, a smoke note. Brew it like any other souchong, and don't be precious about it.

There is a lower step still: low-grade gongfu smoked afterwards and sold as smoked souchong, sometimes called 'false souchong'. For a buyer, the practical point is that 'Lapsang' on a label does not by itself mean Tongmu. Ask where it was made.
history:
The name exists because of the distinction it draws. Zheng Shan, 'true mountain', marked the Tongmu teas of Chong'an, and other districts copying them were grouped as Waishan or Rengong Xiaozhong.

Little is documented about when each district began making it or who led the way, and the boundaries between these terms vary between accounts.
